‘Wehave produced three lines of transgenic mice that
contain additional copies of the mouse phosphoglycer-
ate kinase 1 (PgkI) gene. Two of these lines, 94-A and
‘which are descendants of a common founder, did
not produce liveborn progeny carrying two copies of
these transgenes (i-e., N/A, KIK, or A/K). Genotyping of
midgestation embryos showed that A/K embryos are
dead by Embryonic Day 10. Comparison of the level
of transgene expression in the three transgenic lines
ruled out PGKI toxicity as the cause of death of M/A,
NK, and K/K embryos, The death of M/A, K/K, and AK
transgenic mice was therefore attributed to an inser~
tional mutation disrupting a gene or genes essential
for normal embryogenesis. Analysis of the structure of
the 94-A and 94-K transgenes indicated that they differ
in the number of tandem repeats and in the positions
of the transgene-cellular DNA junctions. To deter
mine if the two transgenes represent a single integra-
tion followed by a rearrangement or two independent
jegration events, we cloned the endogenous se-
quences surrounding the 94-A and 94-K transgené
sertion sites, Restriction analysis of the isolated geno-
mie clones indicated that the endogenous sequences
abutting the 3" ends of the 94-A and 94-K transgenes
are separated by less than 20 kb, providing strong sup-
port for the single integration model. Further analysis
indicated that the 94-A transgene is associated with a
deletion of at least 18kb and is located in the vicinity of
‘a widely transcribed endogenous gene. Chromosomal
‘mapping of the endogenous sequences flanking the 04

ular basis of existing mouse mutations (spontaneous
or generated by chemical or radiation mutagenesis;
Lyon and Searle, 1989). Defining the chromosomal po-
sition of these mutations with respect to an ever ex-
panding repertoire of molecular markers (Copeland
and Jenkins, 1991; Copeland et al., 1993; Rowe et al.,
1994) makes possible the identification of candidate
genes or the cloning of the affected genes by chromo-
some walking (for a review, see Reith and Bernstein,
1991). Isolating the affected gene, however, is still not
a straightforward task and requires a time-consuming
search for transcribed sequences through vast
stretches of DNA.
One class of mutations circumvents the difficulties
that stand in the way of cloning the affected genes,
‘These mutations are generated by the insertion of DNA
with a known sequence within or near an endogenous
gene. The inserted DNA represents a molecular marker
that allows the cloning of the sequences at the insertion
site and thus significantly simplifies the task of isolat-
ing the affected gene. Several types of agents are
known to cause insertional mutations. Retroviral inser-
tions have been determined to be the cause of some
spontaneous mouse mutations, e¢., dilute, hairless,
and pink-eyed unstable (Mercer ef al., 1991; Stoye et
al., 1988; Brilliant et al., 1991), Retroviral integration
at novel positions in the germ line can also be achieved
experimentally, by mobilizing dormant retroviruses in
certain hybrid crosses (Spence et al, 1989) or by di-
rectly introducing retroviruses into early embryos
(Schnicke et al., 1983; Gridley et al., 1990; Weiher et
al., 1990) or embryonic stem (BS) cells (Conlon et al,
1991). Retroviral integration has been estimated to re-
sult in visible mutations in ~5% of these transgenic
lines. In many of these lines, molecular analysis of the
insertional mutation has led to the cloning of the dis-
rupted endogenous gene (Schnieke et al, 1983; Soriano
et al., 1987; Gridley et al, 1990; Weiher et al., 1990;
‘Zhou et al., 1998; Conlon et al., 1994; DeGregori et al,
1994).

croinjection of DNA into mouse embryos (Brinster and
Palmiter, 1986; Gridley, 1991; Meisler, 1992). Insertion
